title: Student-Generated Examples in the Learning of Mathematics https://tipsforteachers.co.uk/research-student-generated-examples-in-the-learning-of-mathematics/ -- original paper: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/251513468_Student-generated_examples_in_
author: Craig Barton
summary: This Tips for Teachers research summary covers Watson and Mason's study on using student-generated examples, particularly boundary examples, to deepen mathematical understanding of theorems and definitions. The central argument is that students often treat mathematical techniques as mechanical manipulation rather than as an act of constructing an object with specified properties, and that asking students to generate their own examples — especially boundary or 'pathological' ones that test the edges of a definition — surfaces and repairs that gap. The authors present a set of tasks built around a single powerful, reusable strategy: describe a general object, impose constraints, and use those constraints to determine the parameters. They note that students often dismiss unusual boundary examples as irrelevant oddities rather than recognising them as the very cases that reveal why a definition needs the constraints it has. Barton's summary highlights the reframing at the heart of the paper: familiar techniques like solving a differential equation or finding an integral are themselves examples of 'constructing an object with specified properties,' a fact students have practised extensively without ever being told, and making that framing explicit is proposed as a route to deeper conceptual understanding rather than procedural mimicry.
points: Students commonly experience mathematical techniques as mechanical manipulation, missing that a technique like solving an equation is itself an act of 'constructing an object with specified properties.'
Boundary or unusual examples — which students often dismiss as irrelevant 'pathologies' — are reframed as the cases that reveal exactly why a definition or theorem needs the constraints it has.

A single reusable strategy underpins the tasks: describe a general object, impose constraints, and use those constraints to determine parameter values — a strategy the authors argue is 'powerful and pervasive' across mathematics.

The paper's tasks were developed and refined iteratively based on observed student difficulties, with validity judged by whether the approach actually improves teaching practice, not by a controlled trial.

The core teaching implication is to make explicit to students that they are constructing mathematical objects when they apply a technique, since this framing is available in techniques they already use but rarely notice as construction.
quotes: This research article investigates common difficulties students face in mathematics, specifically their understanding of theorems and the use of examples.
The authors propose that encouraging students to generate their own examples, especially boundary cases, improves comprehension and retention.
When students are taught techniques as a set of mechanical manipulations, they may not see the creative problem-solving aspects of the technique.

The authors discuss several strategies for helping students appreciate a particular mathematical example, especially a boundary example that shows why constraints are required in a definition or theorem. Students sometimes dismiss these examples as pathologies.

Any technique which yields answers illustrates ways to construct mathematical objects. Solving a first order linear differential equation, finding an integral, disentangling eigenvalues and eigenvectors for a matrix, and changing basis are all examples of constructing an object with specified properties.
Thus constructing mathematical objects is something students have seen and done a great deal of, yet for the most part they are unaware of it in these terms.
